questions.q: A 28-year-old male presents with a single hypopigmented patch on the forearm with loss of sensation. Slit skin smear is negative. Nerve biopsy shows epithelioid cell granulomas with lymphocytic infiltration but no bacilli. Which type of leprosy does he have?
questions.exp: Tuberculoid leprosy presents with a single well-defined hypopigmented patch, complete loss of sensation, and negative slit skin smear. Nerve biopsy shows well-formed epithelioid granulomas with Langhans giant cells and lymphocytes but no bacilli (paucibacillary). Indeterminate leprosy has no granulomas on biopsy.

questions.q: A leprosy patient on MDT develops sudden onset erythema and oedema of existing skin lesions, fever, and joint pain. There is no new nerve involvement. The most appropriate next step is:
questions.exp: This describes Type 1 lepra reaction (reversal reaction) which requires continuation of MDT along with corticosteroids (prednisolone 40-60 mg/day). MDT must never be stopped during a lepra reaction. Thalidomide is used for ENL (Type 2) in males only.

questions.q: A 35-year-old HIV-positive man presents with multiple nodular skin lesions with central umbilication. Biopsy shows large encapsulated yeasts on mucicarmine stain. The most likely causative agent is:
questions.exp: Cutaneous cryptococcosis in immunocompromised patients presents with molluscum-like umbilicated papules. Biopsy shows large encapsulated yeasts (Cryptococcus neoformans) highlighted by mucicarmine stain (capsule stains red). Histoplasma causes similar lesions but the capsule is not as prominent on mucicarmine.

questions.q: A 45-year-old farmer presents with painless verrucous plaques on the foot with black dots on the surface. Biopsy shows Medlar bodies (sclerotic cells). The treatment of choice is:
questions.exp: Chromoblastomycosis presents with verrucous plaques and is characterized by Medlar bodies (muriform/sclerotic cells) on histology. Oral itraconazole (200-400 mg/day for 6-18 months) is the drug of choice. Potassium iodide is used for sporotrichosis, not chromoblastomycosis.

questions.q: A 19-year-old sexually active female presents with multiple painful vesicles on an erythematous base on the vulva with inguinal lymphadenopathy and dysuria. Which is the most appropriate initial therapy?
opts: Oral valacyclovir 1g twice daily for 10 days
Oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days
questions.exp: Primary genital herpes (HSV-2) presents with painful vesicles, systemic symptoms, and lymphadenopathy. Oral valacyclovir 1g BD for 7-10 days is preferred for primary episode due to better bioavailability. Topical therapy is ineffective for primary HSV. Penicillin treats syphilis; doxycycline treats chlamydia/LGV.

questions.q: A 30-year-old man presents with a painless ulcer on the glans penis with indurated margins, followed by unilateral painless rubbery inguinal lymphadenopathy. VDRL is reactive at 1:64. The most appropriate treatment is:
opts: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM single dose
Procaine penicillin 600,000 units IM daily for 10 days
questions.exp: Primary/secondary syphilis is treated with benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM as a single dose per WHO/NACO guidelines. Doxycycline is an alternative for penicillin allergy (100 mg BD for 14 days). Procaine penicillin daily for 10 days is an alternative but less convenient.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman presents with painless genital ulcers followed by bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy with groove sign (groove between inguinal and femoral nodes). Frei's test is positive. The diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) caused by Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1-L3 presents with a transient painless ulcer followed by inguinal lymphadenopathy with the pathognomonic groove sign (nodes divided by Poupart's ligament). Frei's test is an intradermal Chlamydia antigen test. Treatment is doxycycline 100 mg BD for 21 days.

questions.q: A 60-year-old man presents with tense bullae on normal and erythematous skin, predominantly on the flexures and abdomen. Direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 deposition at the dermoepidermal junction. The diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid is the most common autoimmune blistering disorder in the elderly. Tense subepidermal bullae on flexures with linear IgG/C3 at BMZ on DIF is characteristic. Target antigens are BP180 (type XVII collagen) and BP230. Pemphigus vulgaris shows intraepidermal flaccid blisters with IgG in intercellular spaces.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with flaccid bullae, erosions, and positive Nikolsky sign on the oral mucosa and skin. Histology shows suprabasal acantholysis with 'tombstone' appearance of basal cells. The antibody responsible targets:
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris with mucosal and cutaneous involvement has antibodies against both desmoglein 3 (primarily mucosal) and desmoglein 1 (cutaneous). Dsg1 alone is targeted in pemphigus foliaceus (superficial blisters, no mucosal disease). BP180/BP230 are targeted in bullous pemphigoid.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman presents with intensely pruritic grouped vesicles on the extensor surfaces of elbows and knees. DIF shows granular IgA at dermal papillae. She should be evaluated for:
questions.exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis (DH) presents with intensely pruritic grouped vesicles on extensor surfaces. Granular IgA at dermal papillae tips on DIF is pathognomonic. It is associated with celiac disease in >90% of cases. Treatment is dapsone and gluten-free diet.

questions.q: A 32-year-old woman with SLE develops a butterfly-shaped erythematous rash after sun exposure. ANA is 1:1280, anti-dsDNA strongly positive. The most specific antibody for SLE is:
questions.exp: Anti-Smith (anti-Sm) antibody is highly specific for SLE (~99% specificity) though sensitivity is low (25-30%). Anti-dsDNA is specific and correlates with disease activity/nephritis. Anti-Ro is associated with subacute cutaneous lupus and neonatal lupus. Anti-histone is associated with drug-induced lupus.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman presents with sclerodactyly, Raynaud's phenomenon, telangiectasias, and calcinosis cutis. HRCT shows ILD. Anti-centromere antibody is positive. The diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (lcSSc/CREST syndrome) has skin involvement limited to hands/face/forearms, Raynaud's, and anti-centromere antibodies. Diffuse SSc has truncal skin involvement and anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I). CREST = Calcinosis, Raynaud's, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia.

questions.q: A 40-year-old man presents with proximal muscle weakness, heliotrope rash, Gottron's papules, and elevated creatine kinase. The most feared complication of dermatomyositis in adults is:
questions.exp: Dermatomyositis has a strong association with internal malignancy in adults >40 years (20-30% of cases), particularly ovarian, lung, GI, and breast cancers. All adult patients with new-onset DM must be evaluated for occult malignancy. Anti-MDA5 antibody is associated with rapidly progressive ILD.

questions.q: A 65-year-old man presents with a pearly translucent papule with telangiectasias on the nose. Histology shows palisading nuclei at the periphery of tumor islands with retraction artifact. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Nodular basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is the most common skin cancer. It presents as a pearly papule with telangiectasias and rolled borders. Histology shows palisading of nuclei at the periphery of basaloid tumor islands with retraction artifact (mucin retraction). It is locally destructive but rarely metastasizes.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with an asymmetric pigmented lesion on her back with irregular borders, multiple colors, and diameter 8 mm. Dermoscopy shows irregular pigment network and regression structures. The best next step is:
opts: Punch biopsy of the darkest area
questions.exp: Suspicious melanocytic lesions (ABCDE criteria) require excision biopsy with narrow 1-2 mm margins to allow complete histological assessment including Breslow thickness for staging. Punch or shave biopsy may miss the deepest portion and compromise staging. Imiquimod is not appropriate for suspected melanoma.

questions.q: A 25-year-old man with severe psoriasis is being considered for a TNF-alpha inhibitor. Which of the following is an absolute contraindication?
opts: Mild hepatitis B with undetectable viral load
Previous history of basal cell carcinoma
questions.exp: Active tuberculosis is an absolute contraindication to TNF-alpha inhibitors (adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab) as they markedly increase risk of TB reactivation. All patients must be screened with TST/IGRA and chest X-ray before starting biologics. Active TB must be treated before initiating anti-TNF therapy.

questions.q: A 30-year-old man presents with well-demarcated silvery scaly plaques. Histology shows parakeratosis, Munro microabscesses, and absent granular layer. The most characteristic histological finding specifically associated with psoriasis is:
questions.exp: Munro microabscesses (neutrophilic collections in the stratum corneum) and Kogoj's spongiform pustules (neutrophils in spinous layer) are characteristic of psoriasis. Absent granular layer and regular acanthosis with suprapapillary plate thinning complete the picture. Spongiosis is characteristic of eczema/dermatitis.

questions.q: A 35-year-old atopic patient with lichenified plaques in flexures fails topical steroids. Total IgE is markedly elevated. The most appropriate first-line biologic for moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis is:
questions.exp: Dupilumab (anti-IL-4Ra monoclonal antibody) is the first FDA/EMA-approved biologic for moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis. It blocks both IL-4 and IL-13 signaling. Omalizumab targets IgE and is approved for urticaria. Ustekinumab and secukinumab target IL-12/23 and IL-17 respectively (used in psoriasis).

questions.q: A 50-year-old woman develops grayish-blue pigmentation on the face after using topical hydroquinone for 3 years for melasma. Histology shows banana-shaped ochre-colored deposits in the dermis. This complication is:
questions.exp: Exogenous ochronosis is a paradoxical bluish-gray darkening caused by prolonged use of high-concentration hydroquinone, especially in dark-skinned individuals. Histology shows banana-shaped ochre-colored deposits in the dermis. Treatment involves stopping hydroquinone; laser therapy may help.

questions.q: A 10-year-old boy presents with depigmented macules on the face, wrists, and around body orifices since age 5. Wood's lamp shows chalk-white fluorescence. Family history is positive. The most appropriate initial therapy for generalized vitiligo is:
questions.exp: Narrowband UVB (NB-UVB) phototherapy is the most effective repigmentation therapy for generalized vitiligo and is safe for children. It is preferred over oral PUVA due to lower carcinogenicity risk. Topical tacrolimus is preferred for localized facial vitiligo. Topical steroids are first-line for localized vitiligo in adults.

questions.q: A patient is started on dapsone for dermatitis herpetiformis. Two weeks later he develops hemolytic anemia and methemoglobinemia. Which enzyme deficiency makes him most susceptible to dapsone toxicity?
questions.exp: G6PD deficiency markedly increases susceptibility to dapsone-induced hemolytic anemia and methemoglobinemia. Dapsone causes dose-dependent hemolysis in all patients, but G6PD-deficient individuals are disproportionately affected. G6PD screening before starting dapsone is recommended. Methylene blue treats symptomatic methemoglobinemia.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman with severe cystic acne is started on isotretinoin. The most important monitoring parameters during treatment include:
opts: Fasting lipid profile and liver function tests
questions.exp: Isotretinoin monitoring requires fasting lipid profile (hypertriglyceridemia in ~25%) and liver function tests (hepatotoxicity) at baseline and periodically. Pregnancy testing is mandatory before and during treatment (strict contraception required). CBC is less critical. Renal toxicity is not a primary concern with isotretinoin.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman presents for Mohs micrographic surgery for recurrent BCC on the nasal tip. The key advantage of Mohs surgery over wide local excision is:
opts: Complete peripheral and deep margin assessment with tissue conservation
Better cosmetic outcome in all skin cancers
questions.exp: Mohs micrographic surgery involves sequential excision with immediate frozen section examination of 100% of the surgical margin (peripheral and deep). This allows tissue conservation while ensuring complete excision, ideal for recurrent tumors, ill-defined margins, and cosmetically sensitive areas. Cure rates for recurrent BCC reach 99%.

questions.q: A 28-year-old male presents with multiple flesh-colored pedunculated papules on the shaft of the penis. HPV typing shows HPV 6 and 11. The best initial patient-applied treatment for accessible condylomata acuminata is:
questions.exp: Condylomata acuminata (genital warts) from low-risk HPV 6/11 can be treated with patient-applied podophyllotoxin 0.5% (twice daily for 3 days then 4 days rest, up to 4 cycles) or imiquimod 5% cream. Provider-applied options include cryotherapy and trichloroacetic acid. HPV 16/18 cause high-grade dysplasia and cancer.

questions.q: A 6-year-old child presents with honey-colored crusted lesions around the nose and mouth, rapidly spreading. Gram stain shows gram-positive cocci in clusters. The most common causative organism of non-bullous impetigo is:
questions.exp: Non-bullous impetigo is most commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus (alone or with S. pyogenes). It presents with honey-colored crusted lesions around the mouth and nose. Bullous impetigo is caused exclusively by S. aureus (phage type 71) producing exfoliative toxin A. Treatment is topical mupirocin or fusidic acid; systemic antibiotics for extensive disease.

questions.q: A 50-year-old diabetic presents with rapidly progressive erythema and severe pain of the lower leg disproportionate to appearance. CT shows gas in subcutaneous tissue. The most appropriate immediate management is:
opts: Emergency surgical debridement and broad-spectrum IV antibiotics
IV antibiotics alone and close monitoring
questions.exp: Necrotizing fasciitis is a life-threatening surgical emergency. Gas in subcutaneous tissue on CT is pathognomonic. Immediate surgical debridement combined with broad-spectrum IV antibiotics covering gram-positive, gram-negative, and anaerobic organisms is mandatory. Hyperbaric oxygen may be adjunctive but does not replace surgery.

questions.q: A 40-year-old man presents with multiple violaceous plaques on the lower legs and oral mucosa. Biopsy shows spindle cell proliferation with slit-like vascular spaces and extravasated RBCs. HHV-8 immunostaining is positive. He is HIV positive with CD4 of 80. First-line therapy for cutaneous-only Kaposi's sarcoma is:
questions.exp: AIDS-associated Kaposi's sarcoma (HHV-8) responds dramatically to effective ART, which reconstitutes immune function and often leads to regression. For limited cutaneous-only disease, optimizing ART is first-line. Systemic chemotherapy (pegylated liposomal doxorubicin or paclitaxel) is for extensive or visceral disease.

questions.q: A neonate develops widespread blistering after minimal trauma. EM shows cleavage within the lamina lucida of the basement membrane zone. The gene most likely mutated in the severe (Herlitz) form of junctional epidermolysis bullosa is:
questions.exp: Junctional EB has cleavage within the lamina lucida. The Herlitz (lethal) form is caused by mutations in laminin-332 genes (LAMA3, LAMB3, LAMC2), resulting in complete absence of laminin-332. COL7A1 mutations cause dystrophic EB (sublamina densa cleavage). Keratin 5/14 mutations cause EB simplex (intraepidermal). Plectin mutations cause EB simplex with muscular dystrophy.

questions.q: A 22-year-old student presents with annular scaly patches on the trunk with central clearing. KOH shows branching hyphae. She does not respond to topical clotrimazole after 4 weeks. The next best management is:
opts: Oral itraconazole 200 mg daily for 2 weeks
Perform fungal culture and discontinue treatment
questions.exp: Tinea corporis unresponsive to topical azoles requires systemic antifungal therapy. Oral itraconazole (200 mg/day for 1-2 weeks) is preferred for widespread or treatment-resistant tinea. Oral terbinafine (250 mg/day for 2 weeks) is an effective alternative. Switching topical agents is unlikely to succeed after 4 weeks of failed treatment.

questions.q: A 70-year-old immunosuppressed patient develops a rapidly growing keratotic nodule with central crater on the lower lip over 6 weeks. Which management is most appropriate?
opts: Observation for 3 months for spontaneous regression
questions.exp: A rapidly growing keratotic nodule on the lip in an immunosuppressed patient has high likelihood of squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) with significant metastatic potential. Excision biopsy with adequate margins and histopathological examination is mandatory to distinguish SCC from keratoacanthoma and guide further management.

questions.q: A 50-year-old man presents with erythematous scaly plaques on the scalp, elbows, and knees, nail pitting, and onycholysis. Auspitz sign is positive. The biological basis for the Auspitz sign in psoriasis is:
opts: Removal of scales exposes dilated tortuous capillaries in elongated dermal papillae causing pinpoint bleeding
Removal of scales reveals moist weeping erosions due to spongiosis
Removal of scales reveals milia due to trapped keratin
Removal of scales causes positive Nikolsky sign due to acantholysis
questions.exp: The Auspitz sign consists of pinpoint bleeding after removal of the last scales in psoriasis. This occurs because psoriatic plaques have elongated dermal papillae containing dilated, tortuous capillaries close to the surface. When scales are removed, these capillaries are disrupted causing punctate bleeding. The suprapapillary epidermis is very thin.
